Superscript Generator

Raised letters and digits for exponents, units and footnotes

Raised characters, and the eight capitals Unicode skipped

Unicode never set out to provide a superscript alphabet, so what exists is leftovers: ¹ ² ³ inherited from Latin-1 and a scattering of raised letters borrowed from phonetic notation. The gaps are real and permanent. Capitals C, F, Q, S, V, X, Y and Z have no superscript form at all, and lowercase q has none either, so this site leaves those letters at full height rather than dropping a blank into your sentence. Digits are the exception, complete from ⁰ to ⁹.

Where it earns its keep is any field with no formatting to offer: a listing that needs 45 m², a message carrying x², a footnote mark after a claim in a bio. None of this is styling applied to a letter. Each raised character is its own codepoint that happens to be drawn small and high, which is how it survives the trip into a spreadsheet cell. It is also finer than real superscript type, worth checking before you set anything small in it.

Also searched as: small text above, exponent generator, raised letters, tiny text.

Where Superscript text works, and where it does not

WorksReads as ordinary text everywhere, because these are normal Unicode letters rather than a maths alphabet. Watch outUnicode has no character for every letter in this style, so the missing ones stay plain. That is the honest fallback, not a fault.

Superscript questions

Which letters are missing?

Capitals C, F, Q, S, V, X, Y and Z have no superscript form anywhere in Unicode, and lowercase q has none either. Those characters stay at full size rather than becoming a blank, so a word containing them comes out uneven. Digits are the reliable part, with nought to nine all present.

How do I type an exponent like x squared?

Run the number through and place it after the base, so x followed by a raised two gives you x². The same approach handles units: a square metre becomes m² and a cubic one m³. It is notation for people to read, not something a calculator or a spreadsheet formula will evaluate.

Why does it look smaller than superscript in a word processor?

Because a word processor shrinks and raises the real letter, scaling whatever font you chose. Here the small shape is baked into the character by whoever drew the typeface, at whatever size they settled on. The result is usually finer and a little lighter, which matters in small print.
